macroTrends.title: Macro Trends: From Single-Turn Copilots to Agentic Collectives
macroTrends.disclaimer: ⚠️ [AI-Generated Synthesis Notice]: Macro trends are synthesized by AI from cross-sectional academic literature and empirical benchmarks for executive decision-support.
points: Delegation Over Tool Use: Organizational computing is shifting from passive software artifacts subordinate to human agency toward goal-directed agentic systems capable of task decomposition, external tool invocation, and recursive sub-agent delegation.

Context Architecture as Organizational Design: Multi-agent collectives rely on persistent state traces, schemas, validators, and standardized protocols (such as MCP) rather than human socialization—making context engineering a core determinant of coordination cost.

Principal-Agent Risks & Bounded Autonomy: Recursive delegation introduces classic moral hazard, compounding error cascades, and scope escalation, prompting organizations to enforce bounded autonomy and external authorization chains.

topicRelevance.title: Topic Relevance Today: Agentic AI & Multi-Agent Organizing
topicRelevance.verdict: High-priority frontier research area: enterprise deployment has pivoted from single-prompt chatbots to multi-step agentic workflows, creating urgent gaps in organizational design, principal-agent theory, and delegation accountability.
topicRelevance.worthLookingInto: Yes—emphatically so. As of late 2026, agentic workflows have crossed from prototype benchmarks into production software engineering, procurement, and analytical orchestration, yet management and IS theories lag behind technical capability.
topicRelevance.publishingTrends: Explosive growth since 2023 across NeurIPS/ICLR/ACL (architectures & benchmarks like ReAct, MetaGPT, SWE-agent, OSWorld) and rapid migration into top management and IS outlets (MIS Quarterly 2025 delegation/ecology theories; 2025–2026 arXiv economics & organizational behavior papers).
topicRelevance.topResearchers: Aaron Baird & Likoebe Maruping (agentic IS delegation); Joon Sung Park & Michael S. Bernstein (generative agents); John J. Horton, Gillian Hadfield & Andrew Koh (agentic economic systems); Thomas Grisold, Nicholas Berente & Stefan Seidel (human-AI ecologies); Marta Stelmaszak & Carsten Sørensen (algorithmic delegation); Shunyu Yao (ReAct/Tau-bench); Nenad Tomašev & Simon Osindero (intelligent delegation).
topicRelevance.futureTrend: Convergence of organizational economics (incomplete contracting, nested principal-agent models) with formal multi-agent authorization protocols, shifting research focus from 'can an agent finish a benchmark task' to 'how hybrid human-agent organizations allocate liability, authority, and verification bandwidth.'
topicRelevance.researcherRelevance: Highly relevant for management, IS, economics, and systems scholars. Caution: pure prompt-wrapper benchmarks age out within 6–12 months as base models absorb scaffolding; enduring academic contributions must anchor on structural mechanisms (delegation boundaries, transaction costs, liability, or field RCTs) rather than model-specific tricks.
topicRelevance.coreOutcomes: Formal frameworks for human-agent delegation and bounded autonomy; empirical measurement of error cascades and verification overhead in multi-agent teams; economic models of emergent agent markets; and organizational architectures that preserve human accountability.

papers.title: The Next Generation of Research on IS Use: A Theoretical Framework of Delegation to and from Agentic IS Artifacts
papers.authors: Aaron Baird, Likoebe M. Maruping (MIS Quarterly)
papers.teaser: Foundational IS theory relaxing the assumption of passive human-controlled tools to model bidirectional delegation between human actors and autonomous agentic IS artifacts.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Formulates an agentic IS delegation framework specifying agent endowments, preferences, and roles alongside appraisal, distribution, and coordination mechanisms.
Methodology & Sample: Conceptual and theoretical synthesis reframing three decades of Information Systems use literature for autonomous software artifacts.
Empirical Findings: Establishes analytical propositions distinguishing passive tool use from reciprocal delegation where software can both receive and initiate task transfers.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Highlights how agency shifts from unilateral human control toward negotiated human-agent task boundaries and shared accountability.
Executive & Practical Implications: Guides system designers and managers to explicitly specify decision rights and handoff protocols before deploying autonomous software.

papers.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
papers.authors: Shunyu Yao, Jeffrey Zhao, Dian Yu, Nan Du, Izhak Shafran, Karthik Narasimhan, Yuan Cao (ICLR / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Seminal agent architecture interleaving verbal chain-of-thought reasoning with external environment actions to mitigate hallucination and enable verifiable tool use.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Unifies internal reasoning traces and external API/environment actions in a single interleaved decision loop.
Methodology & Sample: Experimental evaluation across multi-hop question answering, fact verification, and interactive decision-making benchmarks.
Empirical Findings: Outperforms reasoning-only and action-only baselines by grounding intermediate reasoning steps in external retrieved observations.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Produces human-inspectable thought-action-observation trajectories that improve auditability and failure diagnosis.
Executive & Practical Implications: Forms the foundational loop underlying enterprise agentic copilots, retrieval agents, and auditable workflow automation.

papers.title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
papers.authors: Joon Sung Park, Joseph C. O'Brien, Carrie J. Cai, Meredith Ringel Morris, Percy Liang, Michael S. Bernstein (ACM UIST)
papers.teaser: Landmark architecture equipping LLM agents with episodic memory streams, reflection, and hierarchical planning to produce coherent emergent social coordination.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Combines a natural-language memory stream, relevance-recency-importance retrieval, periodic reflection synthesis, and dynamic planning.
Methodology & Sample: Controlled interactive sandbox of 25 generative agents inhabiting a simulated town ('Smallville') with human-evaluated behavioral believability.
Empirical Findings: Agents spontaneously diffused invitations, coordinated group events, and formed persistent social relationships without scripted rules.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Demonstrates that structured memory reflection transforms stateless language models into temporally coherent organizational actors.
Executive & Practical Implications: Enables organizational researchers and managers to prototype social coordination dynamics and policy rollouts in synthetic sandboxes.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Simulated Economic Agents: What Can We Learn from Homo Silicus?
papers.authors: John J. Horton (NBER / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Introduces 'Homo silicus'—using LLMs endowed with endowments and constraints to simulate behavioral economic experiments and market responses before costly field trials.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Treats pretrained LLMs as implicit computational models of human economic decision-making conditioned on scenario endowments.
Methodology & Sample: Replicates classic behavioral economics experiments (fairness, minimum wage, status quo bias) across prompt-varied synthetic cohorts.
Empirical Findings: Synthetic agents qualitatively reproduce directional comparative statics observed in landmark human behavioral experiments.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Exposes both the promise of rapid experimental pre-testing and the risk of training-corpus bias distorting synthetic behavior.
Executive & Practical Implications: Gives researchers and strategy teams a low-cost simulation layer to pilot incentive designs prior to live field experiments.

papers.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
papers.authors: Timo Schick, Jane Dwivedi-Yu, Roberto Dessì, Roberta Raileanu, Maria Lomeli, et al. (NeurIPS / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Demonstrates how language models can autonomously learn when and how to invoke external calculators, search engines, and calendars via self-supervised loss filtering.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Self-supervised API-call learning selecting external tool invocations that strictly reduce next-token prediction loss.
Methodology & Sample: Evaluation across arithmetic, QA, multilingual, and temporal reasoning benchmarks using tool-augmented 6.7B models.
Empirical Findings: Tool-augmented compact models substantially outperform much larger unassisted models on deterministic computation and factual lookup.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Marks the architectural separation between probabilistic language reasoning and deterministic enterprise system execution.
Executive & Practical Implications: Underscores that enterprise agent reliability depends on binding probabilistic models to deterministic APIs.

papers.title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for 'Mind' Exploration of Large Language Model Society
papers.authors: Guohao Li, Hasan Abed Al Kader Hammoud, Hani Itani, Dmitrii Khizbullin, Bernard Ghanem (NeurIPS / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Introduces role-playing with inception prompting to coordinate autonomous assistant-user agent pairs across complex coding and planning tasks.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Structured role-playing communication pairing an AI User (task director) and AI Assistant (executor) constrained by inception prompts.
Methodology & Sample: Large-scale conversational multi-agent datasets across software development, scientific workflows, and decision tasks.
Empirical Findings: Role specialization sustains goal alignment across multi-turn dialogues while exposing failure modes like conversation loops and role flipping.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Shows how explicit role boundaries stabilize autonomous division of labor without continuous human prompting.
Executive & Practical Implications: Highlights the necessity of termination criteria and supervision guards in automated multi-agent loops.

papers.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Noah Shinn, Federico Cassano, Edward Berman, Ashwin Gopinath, Karthik Narasimhan, Shunyu Yao (NeurIPS / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Equips language agents with verbal self-reflection stored in episodic memory, improving sequential task success without updating model weights.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Replaces scalar gradient updates with linguistic self-critique retained across trial episodes.
Methodology & Sample: Evaluated across sequential decision-making (AlfWorld), reasoning (HotpotQA), and code synthesis (HumanEval) benchmarks.
Empirical Findings: Achieves substantial pass-rate gains over single-pass baselines by converting execution failures into actionable verbal heuristics.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Mirrors organizational after-action reviews, encoding tacit error lessons into inspectable natural-language context.
Executive & Practical Implications: Demonstrates how organizations can accumulate operational reliability via structured agent memory rather than costly retraining.

papers.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
papers.authors: Shunyu Yao, Dian Yu, Jeffrey Zhao, Izhak Shafran, Thomas L. Griffiths, Yuan Cao, Karthik Narasimhan (NeurIPS / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Generalizes linear chain-of-thought prompting into tree search with lookahead evaluation and backtracking over coherent reasoning branches.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Frames problem solving as heuristic tree search (BFS/DFS) over intermediate language 'thoughts' with self-evaluation.
Methodology & Sample: Controlled comparisons on combinatorial planning, creative writing coherence, and multi-step deduction puzzles.
Empirical Findings: Raises task success dramatically on problems requiring non-myopic planning and revision where greedy decoding fails.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Parallels dual-process cognitive theory (System 2 deliberation) through inference-time compute allocation.
Executive & Practical Implications: Clarifies cost-accuracy trade-offs when managers deploy higher-latency deliberative agents for high-stakes planning.

papers.title: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
papers.authors: Guanzhi Wang, Yuqi Xie, Yunfan Jiang, Ajay Mandlekar, Chaowei Xiao, Yuke Zhu, Linxi Fan, Anima Anandkumar (TMLR / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Demonstrates lifelong skill accumulation in open-ended environments through an automatic curriculum and a growing library of verified executable routines.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Combines automatic task curriculum generation, iterative code-execution verification, and a persistent vector-indexed skill library.
Methodology & Sample: Open-ended exploration experiments in Minecraft measuring technology-tree progression and zero-shot generalization.
Empirical Findings: Achieves far broader exploration and faster capability compounding than memoryless or RL-only agents.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Operationalizes organizational routine codification—turning one-off problem solving into reusable modular competencies.
Executive & Practical Implications: Illustrates how enterprise agents gain compounding value when verified tool scripts are curated into organizational skill libraries.

papers.title: ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development
papers.authors: Chen Qian, Wei Liu, Hongzhang Liu, Nuo Chen, Yufan Dang, et al. (ACL / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Models a virtual software firm using specialized CEO, CTO, programmer, and tester agents coordinating through structured waterfall chat chains.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Decomposes software production into sequential atomic subtasks negotiated between dyadic role agents ('chat chains').
Methodology & Sample: End-to-end generation and debugging across dozens of standalone software specifications with automated execution checks.
Empirical Findings: Role-separated critique and self-debugging reduce syntax defects and hallucinated dependencies compared to single-agent prompting.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Emulates functional division of labor and peer review loops inside a purely synthetic organizational topology.
Executive & Practical Implications: Provides an experimental testbed for studying how organizational structure shapes automated software output quality.

papers.title: WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents
papers.authors: Shuyan Zhou, Frank F. Xu, Hao Zhu, Xuhui Zhou, Robert Lo, et al. (ICLR / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Self-hosted realistic web benchmark spanning e-commerce, forums, GitLab, and CMS apps revealing sharp reliability gaps in autonomous browser agents.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Evaluates long-horizon autonomous execution inside stateful, multi-domain enterprise web applications.
Methodology & Sample: 812 reproducible web tasks across four realistic functional environments with programmatic state verification.
Empirical Findings: Early frontier LLM agents achieved modest end-to-end success (~14%) relative to human baselines (~78%), failing on state tracking and recovery.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Exposes the gap between static benchmark accuracy and open-ended execution across messy real-world software interfaces.
Executive & Practical Implications: Warns leaders against premature autonomous deployment without deterministic verification and rollback controls.

papers.title: MetaGPT: Meta Programming for a Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
papers.authors: Sirui Hong, Mingchen Zhuge, Jonathan Chen, Xiawu Zheng, Yuheng Cheng, et al. (ICLR / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Encodes formal human Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and structured intermediate artifacts into multi-agent workflows to curb cascading hallucinations.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Replaces unstructured agent chat with SOP-governed roles communicating via standardized intermediate documents (PRDs, API specs, designs).
Methodology & Sample: Empirical benchmarking on software generation suites (HumanEval, MBPP, SoftwareDev) against single-agent and chat-based baselines.
Empirical Findings: Structured artifact handoffs significantly improve end-to-end executability and architectural coherence over free-form agent dialogue.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Demonstrates that classical bureaucratic standardization (SOPs and interface contracts) stabilizes probabilistic multi-agent collectives.
Executive & Practical Implications: Shows engineering managers that multi-agent reliability relies on formal interface schemas rather than open-ended agent chatter.

papers.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
papers.authors: Qingyun Wu, Gagan Bansal, Jieyu Zhang, Yiran Wu, Beibin Li, et al. (arXiv)
papers.teaser: Proposes customizable conversable agents integrating LLMs, code execution, and human-proxy oversight nodes into programmable conversation topologies.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Unifies agent orchestration around standardized message-passing interfaces with configurable human-proxy intervention points.
Methodology & Sample: Case evaluations across mathematical problem solving, coding, retrieval QA, and multi-agent supply-chain decision tasks.
Empirical Findings: Programmable conversation patterns outperform static single-agent prompts by enabling dynamic tool execution and human escalation.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Embeds human-in-the-loop checkpoints directly as first-class participants inside multi-agent message graphs.
Executive & Practical Implications: Provides an architectural blueprint for inserting supervisory approval gates within automated enterprise workflows.

papers.title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
papers.authors: Xiao Liu, Hao Yu, Hanchen Zhang, Yifan Xu, Xuanyu Lei, et al. (ICLR / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Multi-environment benchmark across OS terminals, databases, knowledge graphs, and web tasks exposing steep capability drops in long-horizon agent execution.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Multi-dimensional agent evaluation suite spanning eight interactive environments requiring multi-turn state tracking.
Methodology & Sample: Systematic benchmarking across 25+ commercial and open-weight models on terminal, SQL, web, and game environments.
Empirical Findings: Even top models struggle with multi-turn instruction adherence, error recovery, and strict environment formatting constraints.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Quantifies the capability gap between commercial frontier APIs and open-weight models in interactive agency.
Executive & Practical Implications: Helps technical leaders benchmark whether agentic reliability meets production thresholds before automating back-office pipelines.

papers.title: A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents
papers.authors: Lei Wang, Chen Ma, Xueyang Feng, Zeyu Zhang, Hao Yang, et al. (Frontiers of Computer Science)
papers.teaser: Comprehensive taxonomy decomposing LLM autonomous agents into four core architectural pillars: Profiling, Memory, Planning, and Action.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Establishes a unified four-module reference architecture (Profile, Memory, Planning, Action) for autonomous language agents.
Methodology & Sample: Systematic synthesis of over a hundred agent architectures across social simulation, engineering, and natural-science domains.
Empirical Findings: Identifies memory retrieval bottlenecks, planning horizon decay, and evaluation subjectivity as primary structural constraints.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Connects computational agent design directly to social-science simulation needs and human-aligned role specialization.
Executive & Practical Implications: Provides a shared vocabulary for engineering architects and behavioral researchers evaluating agentic platforms.

papers.title: GAIA: A Benchmark for General AI Assistants
papers.authors: Grégoire Mialon, Clémentine Fourrier, Craig Swift, Thomas Wolf, Yann LeCun, Thomas Scialom (ICLR / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Benchmark of 466 real-world multi-step tasks conceptually simple for humans (~92% accuracy) yet highly challenging for tool-augmented AI assistants.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Evaluates real-world assistant robustness across web retrieval, multi-modality, code execution, and unambiguous fact synthesis.
Methodology & Sample: 466 human-curated questions stratified into three complexity levels with exact unambiguous ground-truth answers.
Empirical Findings: Demonstrated a massive initial human-AI gap (~92% human vs. ~15% early GPT-4 plugins), catalyzing subsequent agentic search breakthroughs.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Highlights how minor tool-use or retrieval errors early in a chain invalidate entire downstream assistant outputs.
Executive & Practical Implications: Supplies a realistic readiness yardstick for knowledge-work automation beyond synthetic academic exams.

papers.title: OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments
papers.authors: Tianbao Xie, Danyang Zhang, Jixuan Chen, Xiaochuan Li, Siheng Zhao, et al. (NeurIPS / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Scalable real-OS benchmark across Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS apps exposing the fragility of vision-language GUI agents on cross-application office tasks.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Tests end-to-end computer-use agents operating directly over real operating systems, GUIs, and bash/file workflows.
Methodology & Sample: 369 open-ended multi-app tasks evaluated inside virtualized OS environments with execution-based verification.
Empirical Findings: Initial multimodal agents succeeded on ~12% of tasks versus >72% for humans, struggling with GUI grounding and multi-app context switching.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Demonstrates why standardized APIs (such as MCP) outperform fragile pixel-level GUI automation in enterprise settings.
Executive & Practical Implications: Guides CIOs deciding between brittle screen-scraping computer agents and API-governed agent integrations.

papers.title: SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
papers.authors: John Yang, Carlos E. Jimenez, Alexander Wettig, Kilian Lieret, Shunyu Yao, Karthik Narasimhan, Ofir Press (NeurIPS / arXiv)
papers.teaser: Introduces Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) design principles, proving that tailoring command interfaces for AI agents rivals raw model scaling on real GitHub bug resolution.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Formulates Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) ergonomics—compact, error-tolerant file viewers, linters, and search tools designed specifically for LM agents.
Methodology & Sample: Controlled evaluations on SWE-bench and HumanEvalFix comparing generic bash shells against ACI-optimized interfaces.
Empirical Findings: Purpose-built ACI design substantially boosts autonomous GitHub issue resolution rates across identical underlying foundation models.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Parallels Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) ergonomics—demonstrating that interface design co-determines agent competence.
Executive & Practical Implications: Engineering platforms must optimize internal tooling, linters, and feedback loops for agentic ergonomics alongside human DevEx.

papers.title: Tau-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
papers.authors: Shunyu Yao, Noah Shinn, Pedram Razavi, Karthik Narasimhan (arXiv)
papers.teaser: Evaluates tool-using agents interacting dynamically with simulated users under strict domain policies, exposing severe pass^k consistency failures.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Measures both single-run accuracy and pass^k reliability consistency across multi-turn user dialogues and database-mutating APIs.
Methodology & Sample: Realistic retail and airline customer-service policy benchmarks pairing LLM-simulated users with stateful backend APIs.
Empirical Findings: Even top models that solve a task once fail dramatically on pass^8 consistency and violate complex compound business policies.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Highlights how probabilistic policy adherence degrades rapidly across repeated real-world enterprise transactions.
Executive & Practical Implications: Requires deterministic rule engines and hard policy enforcement layers outside model prompts for customer-facing agents.

papers.title: Generative Agent Simulations of 1,000 People
papers.authors: Joon Sung Park, Carolyn Q. Zou, Aaron Shaw, Benjamin Mako Hill, Carrie Cai, Meredith Ringel Morris, Robb Willer, Percy Liang, Michael S. Bernstein (arXiv)
papers.teaser: Constructs 1,052 interview-grounded generative agents replicating human survey and behavioral experiment responses with 85% normalized fidelity.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Grounds generative agent personas in two-hour qualitative life interviews rather than crude demographic stereotypes.
Methodology & Sample: 1,052 real U.S. participants interviewed and re-tested two weeks later against their interview-conditioned agent twins across surveys and behavioral games.
Empirical Findings: Interview-grounded agents replicate participants' General Social Survey responses at 85% of human test-retest consistency and outperform demographic-only personas.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Bridges qualitative interview depth with computational multi-agent simulation while identifying limits on nuanced behavioral games.
Executive & Practical Implications: Opens new mixed-methods research and organizational policy-testing capabilities while raising informed-consent governance questions.

papers.title: When Algorithms Delegate to Humans: Exploring Human-Algorithm Interaction at Uber
papers.authors: Marta Stelmaszak, Mareike Möhlmann, Carsten Sørensen (MIS Quarterly)
papers.teaser: Empirical MIS Quarterly study reversing traditional delegation assumptions by analyzing how autonomous platform algorithms delegate tasks, timing, and risk to human workers.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Extends agentic IS delegation theory by conceptualizing reversed delegation from algorithmic dispatch engines to human workers.
Methodology & Sample: Qualitative field investigation of Uber drivers navigating opaque algorithmic dispatch, pricing, and routing delegations.
Empirical Findings: Identifies how workers interpret, contest, and selectively accept algorithmic delegations under asymmetric information.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Shows that reversed delegation reshapes worker autonomy through temporal nudges, opacity, and automated performance feedback.
Executive & Practical Implications: Warns platform designers that opaque algorithm-to-human task routing breeds distrust and strategic gaming.

papers.title: Guardrails for Human-AI Ecologies: Norm-Based Coordination and Design for Predictability
papers.authors: Thomas Grisold, Nicholas Berente, Stefan Seidel (MIS Quarterly)
papers.teaser: MIS Quarterly design theory combining predictive processing and social norm theory to govern unpredictable interactions in shared human-AI ecologies.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Integrates predictive processing theory with organizational norm theory to design predictability in co-constituted human-AI environments.
Methodology & Sample: Formal information systems design-theory development addressing unstructured multi-agent and human coordination settings.
Empirical Findings: Derives testable design principles for encoding, surfacing, monitoring, and dynamically updating coordination norms as operational guardrails.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Treats norms—rather than rigid rules alone—as adaptive alignment interfaces when autonomous agents act in open contexts.
Executive & Practical Implications: Gives system architects an institutional framework for governing emergent agent behavior alongside human teams.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Collaboration Mechanisms: A Survey of LLMs
papers.authors: Khanh-Tung Tran, Dung Dao, Minh-Duong Nguyen, Quoc-Viet Pham, Barry O'Sullivan, Hoang D. Nguyen (arXiv)
papers.teaser: Synthesizes coordination structures (centralized, decentralized, hierarchical), collaboration strategies, and collective memory mechanisms in LLM multi-agent systems.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Categorizes multi-agent collaboration along actors, collaboration modes (cooperative/competitive/coopetitive), structures, and protocols.
Methodology & Sample: Comprehensive cross-domain review of 2023–2025 LLM multi-agent coordination architectures and communication topologies.
Empirical Findings: Compares centralized orchestrators against peer-to-peer and hierarchical topologies across token efficiency and error resilience.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Connects computational message-passing protocols directly to organizational coordination trade-offs.
Executive & Practical Implications: Assists technical leaders in selecting minimal-overhead multi-agent topologies matched to task interdependence.

papers.title: From LLM Reasoning to Autonomous AI Agents: A Comprehensive Review
papers.authors: Mohamed Amine Ferrag, Norbert Tihanyi, Mérouane Debbah (arXiv)
papers.teaser: Consolidates reasoning mechanisms, agent-to-tool protocols (MCP), and agent-to-agent interoperability standards (A2A/ACP) shaping modern agent ecosystems.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Maps the architectural evolution from standalone prompt reasoning to standardized interoperable multi-agent protocol stacks.
Methodology & Sample: Comprehensive technical review of 2019–2025 reasoning benchmarks, toolkits, and emerging open agent protocols.
Empirical Findings: Documents how standardized tool and agent interfaces (MCP, A2A) reduce custom integration glue while creating new cross-agent attack surfaces.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Illustrates how open interoperability standards shift agent ecosystems from monolithic silos toward modular service markets.
Executive & Practical Implications: Highlights protocol standardization as a strategic architectural decision for enterprise AI platform teams.

papers.title: An Economy of AI Agents
papers.authors: Gillian K. Hadfield, Andrew Koh (arXiv)
papers.teaser: Economic and legal synthesis examining how markets, contracts, verification infrastructure, and firm boundaries transform when autonomous AI agents transact at scale.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Models an emergent economy populated by autonomous goal-directed software agents executing transactions, negotiations, and long-horizon plans.
Methodology & Sample: Economic theory and institutional design analysis integrating contract theory, mechanism design, and computer science.
Empirical Findings: Identifies asymmetric verification, collusion risks, and identity/reputation bottlenecks as central threats to agentic markets.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Argues that digital economic institutions—not just model weights—determine whether agentic automation generates broad welfare.
Executive & Practical Implications: Calls on platform architects and policymakers to build verifiable agent identity, dispute-resolution, and market-design rails.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Systems Should be Treated as Principal-Agent Problems
papers.authors: Paulius Rauba, Simonas Cepenas (arXiv)
papers.teaser: Reframes multi-agent AI engineering through microeconomic principal-agent theory, modeling asymmetric information, moral hazard, and misaligned sub-agent incentives.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Maps multi-agent delegation hierarchies onto formal principal-agent contracts with hidden information and hidden action.
Methodology & Sample: Theoretical synthesis bridging contract theory, mechanism design, and multi-agent AI failure taxonomies.
Empirical Findings: Shows why purely software-engineering fixes miss emergent moral hazard, specification gaming, and covert misgeneralization across sub-agents.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Uses incentive alignment, monitoring budgets, and contractual verification mechanisms to constrain delegated agent drift.
Executive & Practical Implications: Urges technical leaders to pair agent orchestration code with economic monitoring and audit incentives.

papers.title: Intelligent AI Delegation
papers.authors: Nenad Tomašev, Matija Franklin, Simon Osindero (arXiv)
papers.teaser: Formulates an adaptive delegation framework treating task decomposition as dynamic transfer of authority, responsibility, role boundaries, and trust.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Moves beyond heuristic prompt-routing to formalize delegation across authority transfer, capability verification, accountability, and trust calibration.
Methodology & Sample: Conceptual and systems-architecture synthesis across multi-agent AI networks and human-agent collaboration settings.
Empirical Findings: Demonstrates that robust multi-step execution requires dynamic re-allocation, explicit boundary contracts, and reversible authority grants.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Embeds organizational concepts of accountability and role clarity directly into multi-agent task-routing protocols.
Executive & Practical Implications: Offers enterprise architects a structured protocol for scaling agentic workflows without losing operational control.

papers.title: The Organizational Behavior of Agentic AI: Context, Boundaries, and Collective Intelligence in Human-Agent Workflows
papers.authors: Canhui Liu (arXiv)
papers.teaser: Analyzes agent collectives through organization theory, showing that context architecture—rather than social trust—governs coordination and contextual transaction costs.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Conceptualizes agentic collectives as partial organizational analogues sustained by context architecture (memory, schemas, validators, permissions).
Methodology & Sample: Organization-theoretic analysis contrasting human-imitation multi-agent hierarchies with shared-state adaptive topologies.
Empirical Findings: Naive mimicry of human org charts often underperforms due to lossy handoffs, correlated deliberation, and high verification overhead.
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Introduces 'contextual transaction costs' to explain when shared-state architectures outperform multi-agent message-passing hierarchies.
Executive & Practical Implications: Advises engineering leaders against blindly copying human team structures into multi-agent prompt chains.

papers.title: What to Delegate, What to Preserve: Human Preferences for Agentic AI Across Everyday Life and Work
papers.authors: Sarah Wheeler, Veronica Rammouz, Yaoyao Qian, Zexuan Liu, Mengyi Wei, Anthony Rios, Tianzhi He, Kyrie Zhou (arXiv)
papers.teaser: Empirical scenario study mapping human delegation boundaries across work and personal domains, revealing strong preference for bounded autonomy and retained oversight.
summaryPoints: Core Theoretical Model: Models human agentic preferences along four dimensions—execution delegation, oversight retention, collaborative leadership, and accountability.
Methodology & Sample: Scenario-based empirical survey examining willingness to delegate structured versus high-stakes judgment tasks.
Empirical Findings: Respondents embrace extensive agent execution for routine workflows but insist on retaining final sign-off and boundary control ('bounded autonomy').
Socio-Technical Mechanisms: Demonstrates that perceived loss of moral agency or accountability triggers sharp resistance to fully autonomous delegation.
Executive & Practical Implications: Guides product and HR leaders to build explicit approval checkpoints and reversible execution into workplace agents.
